intro/hello: This lecture is about a second place to spend compute: not while a model is trained, but while it answers.
intro/before: So far, training got all the compute: pretraining, then R L H F, D P O and G R P O. After that, the model answers one token at a time.
intro/more: But the same weights can answer much better if they spend more compute on each question.
intro/long: They can think longer, writing out steps before the answer: a chain of thought.
intro/wide: They can think wider, sampling many answers and voting, or letting a verifier pick one.
intro/smart: And they can think smarter, searching over partial solutions and grading each step.
intro/models: Then come reasoning models, like oh one and R one, trained to do all of this inside one long chain of thought, and finally, thinking budgets and distillation.
serial/puzzle: First, a puzzle. Why should writing out steps help a neural network at all?
serial/fixed: A transformer does a fixed amount of work per token. The input climbs through L layers, and a prediction comes out at the top.
serial/chain: So inside one pass, the longest chain of dependent steps is limited by that depth.
serial/cups: Here is a task that needs a long chain: a ball under five cups, and a list of swaps.
serial/serial: Each swap depends on where the ball ended up after the last one. The work cannot be split up.
serial/cartoon: Picture a cartoon network where every layer does one swap. With three layers, one pass handles three swaps.
serial/fail: Give it eight swaps and demand the answer at once. Five swaps never happen, and here the answer is wrong.
serial/write: Now let it write a token after each pass, saying where the ball is so far.
serial/readback: That token is made at the top of the network and read at the bottom of the next pass, which picks up where the last one stopped.
serial/three: Three passes, three tokens, all eight swaps done, and the answer is right.
serial/formula: So T tokens of thinking give a network with L layers about L times T serial steps instead of L. Theory papers in 2023 and 2024 made this precise.
serial/cost: The price is one full forward pass per token, which is why long thinking is slow and expensive.
cot/seen: A pretrained model has read a lot of worked reasoning: textbook solutions, proofs, answers that explain themselves.
cot/show: So we can ask for that style by showing it. That is chain-of-thought prompting, from Wei and colleagues in 2022.
cot/exemplar: The examples include the reasoning, not just the answer, so the model writes reasoning too.
cot/palm: With eight examples, the 540 billion parameter PaLM set a new state of the art on G S M eight K, grade-school math problems.
cot/emerge: Curiously, it did little for small models, and helped only from around a hundred billion parameters.
cot/zero: Then Kojima and colleagues found the examples were not even needed. One sentence does it: let's think step by step.
cot/numbers: On G S M eight K, that sentence took InstructGPT from about ten percent to about forty one.
cot/extract: A second prompt pulls the final answer out.
cot/caveat: One caution: a chain of thought reads like an explanation, but it is generated text, not always the real reason for the answer.
vote/diff: Sample a chain of thought at a nonzero temperature, and you get a different one every time.
vote/paths: Some take a wrong turn. Many reach the same answer by different routes.
vote/sc: Self-consistency, from Wang and colleagues in 2022, uses this: sample many paths, pull out each final answer,
vote/count: and return the answer that appears most often.
vote/sum: We care about the most likely answer, not the most likely text, and an answer's probability sums over every chain that leads to it.
vote/estimate: Counting votes from samples estimates that sum.
vote/gain: The paper reported large gains, for example almost eighteen points on G S M eight K.
vote/need: Voting needs answers that can be compared, like numbers. For an essay, there is nothing to count.
votemath/simple: How much does voting help? Start simple: each sample is right with probability p, or else the same wrong answer.
votemath/coin: That is like counting heads in n coin flips, and the vote is right when more than half come up right.
votemath/good: With p above one half, more samples help. At point six, one sample is right sixty percent of the time, and a hundred and one samples, ninety eight percent.
votemath/bad: Below one half, the same law works against you: more samples make the wrong answer win more reliably. This is the Condorcet jury theorem, from 1785.
votemath/scatter: But real wrong answers usually scatter: one sample says 125, another 145, another 98.
votemath/weak: A scattered wrong answer rarely wins, so voting can succeed even with p well below one half.
votemath/common: What voting cannot survive is a common mistake: one wrong answer that many samples agree on, with share q.
votemath/flip: Put q above p, and the curve turns over and falls toward zero.
votemath/plural: With many samples, each answer's vote share settles at its probability, so the vote returns the plurality.
votemath/limit: Voting finds the model's favorite answer. If the favorite is wrong, no number of samples will fix it.
coverage/other: Now a different question: is the right answer anywhere among the samples?
coverage/passk: That is pass at k, or coverage: one, minus the chance that all k samples are wrong.
coverage/tries: A problem solved one and a half percent of the time is solved about seventy eight percent of the time in a hundred tries.
coverage/tests: Coverage is what a perfect checker could reach. For code with unit tests, that checker exists.
coverage/est: To measure it, draw n samples, count the c right ones, and use this unbiased estimator from the Codex paper.
coverage/bench: Across a benchmark, coverage keeps climbing, roughly in a straight line against the log of the number of samples.
coverage/why: A benchmark mixes problems the model always solves with problems it solves once in a thousand tries.
coverage/ceiling: Voting, meanwhile, levels off at the share of problems whose right answer is the plurality.
coverage/gap: The gap between the curves is the prize for a good verifier.
bon/verifier: To collect that prize, we need a verifier: something that tells right answers from wrong ones without knowing the answer.
bon/cobbe: Cobbe and colleagues trained one in 2021, alongside G S M eight K: it reads a solution and predicts whether it is right. Their six billion parameter model with a verifier slightly beat a fine-tuned one thirty times larger.
bon/bon: Best-of-n is the simplest use: sample n answers, score each one, keep the top.
bon/noisy: But verifiers are imperfect. Here, right answers score around two, wrong ones around zero, blurred by noise.
bon/exploit: And two percent of wrong answers are exploits, scoring higher than typical right ones.
bon/small: With sixteen samples, the top-scored answer is usually right.
bon/big: With two hundred and fifty six, an exploit is almost surely in the pile, and the verifier picks it.
bon/curve: So accuracy climbs, peaks around sixteen to thirty two samples, and then falls.
bon/goodhart: This is over-optimization again, with no training at all. Gao, Schulman and Hilton measured it in 2022: the proxy score keeps rising while a stronger judge's score peaks and falls.
bon/kl: They measured how far best-of-n moves from the base model with this formula: the log of n, minus n minus one over n.
bon/gentle: A thousand samples move it less than six nats. Best-of-n is a gentle optimizer.
prm/orm: That verifier is an outcome reward model, or O R M: trained on whether the final answer was right, it gives one number per solution.
prm/example: Take this problem: four boxes of twelve markers at two dollars each, eighteen dollars off, split by three classes.
prm/clean: Four checkable steps, ending in twenty six dollars per class.
prm/slip: Put a slip in step two, and every later line inherits it. The outcome check says the answer is wrong, but not where.
prm/prm: A process reward model, or P R M, grades every step instead, and flags step two directly.
prm/cancel: Now make two slips that cancel. The answer is twenty six again.
prm/fooled: An outcome label calls this correct, and an O R M trained on such labels learns to like it. The P R M does not.
prm/product: To score a whole solution, a P R M multiplies its step probabilities: the chance every step is right.
prm/lightman: Lightman and colleagues at OpenAI built one in 2023, from about eight hundred thousand human step labels on competition math.
prm/result: Picking the best of about eighteen hundred samples, their P R M solved about seventy eight percent of a test set, the O R M seventy two, and majority voting seventy.
prm/auto: Later work made step labels automatically: a step is good if completions from it often reach the right answer.
search/guide: A P R M can score a partial solution, so it can guide a search.
search/beam: Beam search over steps keeps the three best partial solutions,
search/expand: extends each with a few sampled next steps,
search/score: scores them all with the P R M, and keeps the best three again.
search/tree: Tree of Thoughts, in 2023, searched trees like this, backing up from dead ends. Monte Carlo tree search is used too.
search/snell: Which way of spending compute is best? In 2024, Snell and colleagues compared them, and compared them with a bigger model.
search/depends: It depends on difficulty. Easy questions did best with revisions of one answer; harder ones needed more sampling or search.
search/fourteen: Choosing per question saved about four times the compute. And where the small model succeeded at least sometimes, extra inference beat a model fourteen times larger.
search/hard: But where the model almost never finds the answer, sampling barely helps. There, a bigger model is the better buy.
search/multiply: Test-time compute multiplies what a model can sometimes do. It cannot create what it cannot do at all.
models/outer: Everything so far wraps an ordinary model in machinery: a sampler, a voter, a verifier, a search.
models/inside: Reasoning models move that machinery inside the model.
models/rl: They are trained with reinforcement learning to write long chains of thought before they answer.
models/behave: In those chains they learn what the outer algorithms did: try an approach, check it, notice a mistake, back up, try another.
models/seq: One long chain becomes a sequential search, with its own verification built in.
models/o1: OpenAI introduced the idea with oh one, in September 2024. It hides its raw chain of thought and shows a summary.
models/axes: It reported accuracy improving smoothly with more R L training compute, and with more thinking time: two new axes to scale.
models/aime: On the 2024 A I M E math competition, it reported about seventy four percent solved with one sample, against about twelve for G P T four oh.
models/r1: DeepSeek R one, in January 2025, published a recipe: G R P O, rewarded only by answers a program can check.
budget/knob: A reasoning model decides how long to think. Most A P Is add a knob: a cap on thinking tokens, or an effort level.
budget/low: Too low a cap cuts reasoning off before an answer. Too high, and you pay for tokens that add nothing.
budget/s1: The s1 paper, in 2025, fine-tuned a model on just a thousand reasoning traces, and controlled its thinking with budget forcing.
budget/cut: To cut thinking short, insert the end-of-thinking marker, and make it answer.
budget/wait: To extend it, hold back the marker and append the word wait, so the model looks at its work again.
budget/rose: Accuracy rose with the forced budget, then flattened out.
budget/toy: Here is a toy. A hard problem needs twelve steps. Until the budget passes twelve it can only guess; after that, re-checks help.
budget/easy: An easy problem, two steps, is done almost at once. Everything after that is overthinking.
budget/drift: And if a re-check can now and then break a right answer, too much thinking even drags accuracy down.
budget/real: Real models do this: o1-style models were found spending hundreds of tokens on two plus three.
budget/train: Rewards that charge a little for length can teach a model to stop when it is done.
distill/cheap: Discovering good reasoning with reinforcement learning is expensive. Copying it is cheap.
distill/teacher: Run a strong reasoning model, the teacher, on many questions, and keep its chains of thought and answers,
distill/filter: often only the ones whose answer checks out.
distill/student: Then train a small student model to predict those tokens: plain next-token prediction on the teacher's text.
distill/r1d: DeepSeek distilled R one into open models from one and a half to seventy billion parameters, with about eight hundred thousand samples.
distill/beat: The distilled thirty two billion model reasoned far better than the same base trained with large-scale reinforcement learning.
distill/few: Others needed far less: s1 used a thousand traces, and LIMO, eight hundred and seventeen.
distill/star: The idea is older. Star, in 2022, had a model teach itself: keep the rationales that reach the right answer, fine-tune, repeat.
distill/limits: The limits: a student is bounded by its teacher, copies its verbosity, and does not learn to explore.
outro/long: To recap. A transformer does a fixed amount of serial work per token, so writing steps buys depth.
outro/vote: Voting finds the plurality. It works when the right answer is the most common one.
outro/verify: The right answer is often in the pile. A verifier can pick it out, but search too hard against an imperfect one and accuracy falls.
outro/prm: Process reward models grade each step, and can guide a search.
outro/rl: Reasoning models learn with reinforcement learning to do all this inside one chain, on a budget that should match the problem.
outro/distill: And their reasoning can be handed to small models by ordinary fine-tuning.
outro/close: The thread through all of it: the same weights, given more compute at answer time, can find answers one quick pass would miss, as long as something can tell a good answer from a bad one.
